where: Section 2, the paragraph beginning "Bursts are the bandwidth trick"
problem: It says one address phase covers several beats and "the slave increments its own address; the address is not re-sent". That is AXI behaviour, not AHB. On AHB every beat of a burst has its own address phase: the master drives the next (incremented or wrapped) address while the previous data phase completes. A student who believes the slave increments the address will misread every AHB timing diagram and will wrongly compare AHB burst efficiency with AXI.
fix: Bursts are the bandwidth trick. HBURST (burst type and length) and HSIZE (bytes per beat) let the master send several beats back to back, but each beat still has its own address phase: the master drives the incremented (or wrapped) address for the next beat while the current data phase runs, so no clock is wasted. Because a burst must not cross a 1 KB boundary, the decoder's slave select stays the same for the whole burst and the slave can prepare the following beats. Sending one start address and letting the slave count is AXI, not AHB.

where: Section 2, the bullet "HRESP reports OKAY, or ERROR over two cycles"
problem: The wording reads as if OKAY also takes two cycles. In AHB, OKAY is a single-cycle response; ERROR and the SPLIT/RETRY responses take two cycles. A student can mis-state the timing in an exam.
fix: HRESP reports OKAY in a single cycle. ERROR takes two cycles, and so do the SPLIT and RETRY responses that a slave uses when it cannot finish at once.
